content_html:
The federal estate tax is charged on what a person owns when they die, after debts, costs and gifts to a spouse or charity are taken off. For deaths in 2026, the first $15,000,000 is covered by the basic exclusion amount, so only very large estates owe anything. Above that, the tax is effectively 40% of every additional dollar. This calculator follows the same steps as the tax computation on Form 706 to estimate what an estate would owe.

How to use the estate tax calculator

  1. What the estate owns: enter current market values, not what was paid. Include retirement accounts and the payout of any life insurance policy the person owned, even when the money goes straight to a named beneficiary. Jointly owned property generally counts at half its value for married couples.
  2. Deductions: debts, mortgages, funeral costs and the legal and executor fees of settling the estate. Anything left to a spouse who is a U.S. citizen, and anything left to charity, is deducted in full.
  3. Lifetime gifts: gifts above the annual exclusion ($19,000 per recipient in 2026) use up part of the same $15,000,000 exclusion, so they are added back before the tax is worked out.
  4. Unused exclusion from a late spouse: if a spouse died earlier and their executor elected portability, the unused part of their exclusion (the DSUE amount) adds to this estate's exclusion.
  5. State estate or inheritance tax: some states tax estates well below the federal threshold. Any state death tax paid is deductible from the federal taxable estate.

How the estate tax is calculated

  1. Add up everything the person owned to get the gross estate.
  2. Subtract debts, funeral and settlement costs, state death taxes, the charitable deduction and the marital deduction to get the taxable estate.
  3. Add lifetime taxable gifts and apply the unified rate schedule, which climbs from 18% to 40%, to get the tentative tax.
  4. Subtract the applicable credit: the tax the same schedule produces on the exclusion amount. For the 2026 basic exclusion of $15,000,000 the credit is $5,945,800.

Because the credit wipes out all the lower brackets, any estate above the exclusion pays a flat 40% on the excess.

Worked example

Using the calculator's starting figures, an estate holds $3,000,000 of real estate, $12,000,000 of investments, $1,000,000 in cash, $2,000,000 in retirement accounts, a $1,000,000 life insurance payout and $500,000 of other assets.

StepAmount
Gross estate$19,500,000
Less debts ($500,000) and settlement costs ($250,000)$18,750,000
Tentative tax on $18,750,000$7,445,800
Less the applicable credit on $15,000,000$5,945,800
Federal estate tax$1,500,000

That is 40% of the $3,750,000 above the exclusion, or 7.7% of the gross estate. If the person had received a full $15,000,000 of unused exclusion from a late spouse, the tax would fall to zero and $11,250,000 of exclusion would remain.

Portability for married couples

When the first spouse dies, the executor can file Form 706 to carry their unused exclusion over to the survivor, even if no tax is due. A couple can then shelter up to $30,000,000 between them at 2026 levels. Portability is not automatic: the election has to be made on a timely filed return, so it is worth discussing with an estate attorney after the first death.

Ways estates reduce the tax

  • Annual exclusion gifts move money out of the estate without using any of the lifetime exclusion.
  • Paying tuition or medical bills directly to the school or provider is not a taxable gift at all.
  • Charitable bequests and charitable trusts reduce the taxable estate dollar for dollar.
  • An irrevocable life insurance trust can keep a large policy payout out of the gross estate.

Limits of this estimate

The figures apply to deaths in 2026; the exclusion is adjusted for inflation from 2027. The calculator assumes no gift tax was paid on earlier gifts, and does not cover the generation-skipping transfer tax, special-use farm valuation, foreign death tax credits or estates of non-residents. Valuing a business or real estate for an estate return usually needs a professional appraisal.

faq.question: What is the estate tax exemption for 2026?
faq.answer: The basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 per person for deaths in 2026, set by the 2025 tax law known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act. It is scheduled to rise with inflation from 2027 rather than fall back to a lower level.

faq.question: Do heirs pay income tax on what they inherit?
faq.answer: Generally not on the inheritance itself. Most inherited assets also get a stepped-up cost basis to their value at death, which removes the built-in capital gain. Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s are the main exception: withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income to the beneficiary.

faq.question: What is the difference between an estate tax and an inheritance tax?
faq.answer: An estate tax is charged on the estate before anything is distributed, which is how the federal tax works. An inheritance tax is charged on the person receiving the money, and only a handful of states have one, usually with lower rates or exemptions for close relatives.

faq.question: Do I need to file an estate tax return if no tax is owed?
faq.answer: A Form 706 is required when the gross estate plus lifetime taxable gifts exceeds the basic exclusion amount, even if deductions bring the tax to zero. Smaller estates of married people often file anyway to elect portability of the unused exclusion.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved.
